verdict.summary: In main(), the directory-image buffer is sized with 'num_images * OPJ_PATH_LEN * sizeof(char)', evaluated in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic. num_images is an unsigned int derived from the contents of the scanned directory (get_num_images). When the directory contains more than UINT_MAX/OPJ_PATH_LEN entries, the multiplication wraps and filename_buf is allocated far smaller than num_images * OPJ_PATH_LEN bytes, while the following loop stores pointers 'filename_buf + i * OPJ_PATH_LEN' for every i < num_images, producing a pointer table whose entries point up to ~4 GB outside the allocation (filename[1] already sits exactly one-past-the-end). This table is passed unvalidated to load_images/get_next_file, yielding heap out-of-bounds writes/reads. No range check, clamp, or size validation exists on any path.

evidence.reason: Root cause: unsigned 32-bit wrap in the allocation size 'num_images * OPJ_PATH_LEN * sizeof(char)'. Simulated trigger: an attacker-controlled directory with 1,048,577 entries makes num_images = 0x100001, so filename_buf = malloc(4096) while the loop stores filename[1] = filename_buf+4096 (one-past-end) and filename[0xFFFFF] = filename_buf+0xFFFFF000 — out-of-domain pointers handed to load_images (line 74) and get_next_file, causing heap out-of-bounds writes. The only guard present ('if (!dirptr->filename_buf)') tests NULL, not size, and 'if (num_images == 0)' (line 78) runs after the loop and only tests zero.

evidence.snippet: num_images = get_num_images(img_fol.imgdirpath);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: num_images is an unsigned int derived from the contents of the scanned directory (filesystem input), i.e., attacker-controlled data; it reaches the wrapped allocation size at lines 63-64 and the pointer-table construction at line 71 with no bound anywhere in this code.

assumptions: OPJ_PATH_LEN is 4096 (upstream OpenJPEG value); it is not defined in the given code — the wrap threshold is UINT_MAX/OPJ_PATH_LEN for whatever its actual value is.
LP64 data model: sizeof(char*) is size_t, so 'num_images * sizeof(char*)' at line 65 does not wrap; on ILP32 both allocations would wrap.

load_images stores each directory entry's file name into the filename[i] slot established by this code's setup loop (the slot contract documented by lines 63-71); the actual byte-level write is inside the not-shown callee.
opj_stream_destroy tolerates a NULL argument (framework semantics, not quotable here).
OPJ_IMF_MAINLEVEL_MAX is 11, matching the 12-element limitMSamplesSec array; if the macro exceeded 11, 'limitMSamplesSec[mainlevel]' would be an out-of-bounds read, but the macro value is not shown.
limitations: NULL dereference: if malloc at line 61 fails, load_images(NULL,...) is called at line 74 with no NULL check on that path; and if malloc at line 65 fails, the loop at line 70 writes through a NULL filename array. Both require OS allocation failure an attacker cannot induce — not promoted to a finding.

Fail-open exit status: 'ret = 0' is set on the '!dirptr->filename_buf' (line 67) and 'load_images(...) == 1' (line 75) error paths, reporting success on failure; the security consequence depends on an unshown consumer of the exit code.

Potential double-free of l_stream in the cod_format default arm would require cod_format to become invalid after a successful iteration; no statement in this code reassigns parameters.cod_format inside the loop, so the trigger is not instantiated.

TOCTOU between get_num_images (line 60) and load_images (line 74) if the directory is mutated between the calls; the overflow consequence occurs in not-shown code (load_images' internal counting) and the race window is not exhibited as two quotable ordered operations here.
Memory leaks: image is leaked on the cod_format default 'continue'; l_codec is leaked when opj_stream_create_default_file_stream fails — no security impact.
dirptr->num_files is never assigned in this code (set only by the not-shown load_images); its value is UNSOURCED and was not used to confirm or demote any candidate.

verdict.summary: The subdomain validation branch is disabled ('if (0)'), so the user-supplied subdomain_prefix is concatenated into the URL host position without any character validation. An attacker-supplied prefix such as 'evil.com#' produces 'https://evil.com#.example.com', whose effective host is the attacker's site (everything after '#' is a fragment; '/' and '?' behave similarly), defeating the documented invariant that the URL to visit stays under the trusted domain.

evidence.reason: The only 'check if subdomain is valid' is the constant-false 'if (0)', making the validation arm dead code; the only live test is an emptiness check ('subdomain_prefix.length() > 0'), which permits arbitrary characters. The unvalidated attacker string is then formatted directly into the URL host position at the snprintf on line 28. Trigger: argv[2] = 'evil.com#' with argv[1] = 'example.com' yields 'https://evil.com#.example.com' — the URL's effective host is the attacker-controlled evil.com, not the trusted domain.

assumptions: No statement in this code validates or attests the 'domain' parameter's actual trustworthiness; its 'trusted' status comes only from the docstring comment, which is intent, not enforcement.

The consumer that 'visits' the returned URL is not shown; however, the defect (unvalidated attacker content placed in the URL host position, defeating the code's own trusted-domain contract) is fully instantiated at line 28 in this code and does not depend on that consumer.
limitations: snprintf buffer overflow was considered and dismissed: every snprintf call passes the fixed bound MAX_URL_LENGTH (256), so the write into url[] is bounded; only silent truncation of oversized input is possible (secondary, not the primary defect).

No outbound HTTP request or redirect/Location header is performed in this code (output is std::cout only), so CWE-601/CWE-918 were deliberately not emitted per mapping rules; CWE-20 names the root cause.

verdict.summary: parse_mb_skip consumes attacker-controlled bitstream values (skip_type from get_bits(&s->gb,2) and per-macroblock skip bits) and writes to s->current_picture_ptr->mb_type at index mb_y * s->mb_stride + mb_x under loop bounds mb_y < s->mb_height / mb_x < s->mb_width. This code contains no guard relating mb_stride to mb_width or to the allocation size of mb_type, and no default arm in the switch; however, every field determining write safety (mb_stride, mb_width, mb_height, current_picture_ptr and its mb_type allocation) and the SKIP_TYPE_* constant values are never assigned or defined in this code. Under the required evidence rules these UNSOURCED values can neither instantiate the harmful precondition (e.g. mb_stride < mb_width) nor serve as a guard, so no candidate's trigger is fully instantiated and no primary vulnerability can be confirmed within the given code.

assumptions: No non-NULL or validity contract for w or s->current_picture_ptr is documented, asserted, or checked in the given code; their soundness is assumed from not-shown initialization.

get_bits/get_bits1 are assumed to be the standard FFmpeg bitreader semantics (returning bits from the input bitstream and saturating safely past the end); the bitstream s->gb is attacker-controlled media content, so w->skip_type (0..3) and all get_bits1 results are attacker-data.
MB_TYPE_* flags are assumed to be plain bit constants; their values are not defined in this code.
SKIP_TYPE_NONE/MPEG/ROW/COL are assumed to be the enum values 0..3 covering the full 2-bit domain of skip_type; this cannot be quoted from the given code.
limitations: Out-of-bounds write candidate (CWE-787/CWE-119): mb_type[mb_y * s->mb_stride + mb_x] is written with no check that mb_stride >= mb_width or that the array holds stride*height entries. The harmful precondition (mb_stride < mb_width or undersized allocation) is UNSOURCED — no statement in this code assigns or constrains s->mb_stride, s->mb_width, s->mb_height, or the mb_type allocation — so the trigger cannot be instantiated. If those invariants are ever violated by not-shown setup code, this loop is an out-of-bounds write sink.

Integer overflow candidate (CWE-190): mb_y * s->mb_stride + mb_x in int can overflow only if stride*height approaches INT_MAX; both operands are UNSOURCED and no concrete harmful value can be computed from this code's constants.

Missing default arm candidate: the switch on the attacker-controlled 2-bit skip_type has no default case; if any of the four case constants were outside 0..3, an unmatched skip_type would leave mb_type unwritten (stale/uninitialized state) whose security impact would occur in not-shown decoder stages; the case-constant values are UNSOURCED and no in-code consumer exists, so this cannot be confirmed.
NULL-dereference candidate (CWE-476): s->current_picture_ptr->mb_type is dereferenced with no NULL check, but no producer of a NULL current_picture_ptr exists in this code.

verdict.summary: decrypt_response copies an attacker-controlled number of bytes (up to 4094, derived from the smart-card response and bounded only against the local 4096-byte plaintext buffer) into the caller-supplied `out` buffer via memcpy without any output-size parameter or bound on any path, enabling an out-of-bounds write. Additionally, in[0]..in[4] are read before the only inlen check, causing an out-of-bounds read when the card returns a short response.

evidence.snippet:
memcpy(out, plaintext, cipher_len - 2);
	*out_len = cipher_len - 2;
evidence.reason: Root cause: memcpy into `out` with length cipher_len-2 (attacker-selectable up to 4094) and no out-capacity parameter or bound anywhere in the function — the only clamp (line 37) bounds cipher_len against sizeof plaintext (4096), not against `out`. Trigger: card returns header 82 01 xx yy 01 with cipher_len up to 4096, decryption fills plaintext, unpad leaves cipher_len at its parsed value, and memcpy writes up to 4094 bytes past a smaller destination (classic buffer overflow via dangerous function).

evidence.snippet:
if (cipher_len < 2 || i+cipher_len > inlen || cipher_len > sizeof plaintext)
		return -1;
evidence.reason: The only length validation bounds cipher_len to [2,4096] against the local plaintext buffer and inlen — it never bounds the copy against the capacity of `out`, and executes only after the header bytes have already been read out of bounds.

Secondary confirmed finding (CWE-125): in[0], in[1], in[2], in[3], in[4] are read (lines 16-28) before the first and only inlen check at line 37; a card response with inlen < 5 (e.g. inlen=2) causes out-of-bounds reads past the response buffer.

assumptions: The line-1 prototype lacks `inlen`; the line-2 signature is taken as the operative definition because the body references inlen.
`in` is assumed to hold inlen valid bytes per the parameter's meaning; reads at indices >= inlen are out of bounds relative to that documented length.

The concrete capacity of `out` in callers is not shown in this code; the finding rests on the structural fact that the interface provides no out-size parameter, so no statement in this code can or does bound the memcpy (recorded as assumption, not used to dismiss).
exdata->smtype and exdata->sk_enc are UNSOURCED (assigned outside this code); both decrypt arms are symmetric so no finding depends on their values.
limitations: A NULL `out_len` passed to this non-static function would dereference at line 54, but no producer of NULL is shown and the trigger is caller-dependent — not counted as a finding.
If every real caller passed an `out` buffer of at least 4096 bytes and always inlen >= 5, impact would reduce to the 3-4 byte OOB read; no statement in the given code establishes either condition.

verdict.summary: In XpmCreateDataFromXpmImage, the buffer pointer `data` is declared (line 9) but never assigned anywhere in the function — the allocation statement that the surrounding code plainly expects (`data = XpmMalloc(data_size); if (!data) RETURN(...)`) is absent, leaving orphaned `RETURN(XpmNoMemory);` bodies. The function then writes through the uninitialized pointer at `*data = (char *) (data + data_nlines);` (line 105) and strcpy's attacker-influenced header strings into pointers derived from it (lines 109-111), an arbitrary-address write / memory-corruption primitive on the exported API's attacker-supplied XpmImage data. A secondary missing check (no bound on `image->height * offset` before `data_size += image->height * offset;`) is also present but its undersized-allocation impact is subsumed by the missing allocation.

evidence.snippet:
data_nlines = header_nlines + image->height + ext_nlines;
    *data = (char *) (data + data_nlines);
evidence.reason: Sink: `data` is written through and used in pointer arithmetic, but no statement anywhere in the function assigns `data` — the required `data = XpmMalloc(data_size)` allocation is missing (its NULL-check body survives as the orphan `RETURN(XpmNoMemory);` above). Writing `*data = ...` through an indeterminate stack value is an arbitrary-address write; the subsequent loop at lines 109-111 (`strcpy(*sptr, *sptr2)` with `sptr = data`) then strcpy's attacker-influenced header lines through it. Trigger instantiated with image{width=8,height=8,ncolors=2,cpp=1}, info=NULL: all quoted checks (lines 32-34, 37-38, 84-86, 88-90, 98-100) pass and control reaches line 105 with `data` unassigned.

evidence.snippet: char **header = NULL, **data, **sptr, **sptr2, *s;
evidence.reason: Origin: `data` is declared without initialization while every sibling used similarly (`header`) is explicitly initialized and later assigned. A full scan of the function body finds no assignment to `data` on any path (the only allocations are `XpmCalloc` for `header` at line 39 and `XpmMalloc` for `*header` at line 68), so the value consumed at line 105 is produced by nothing in this code.

assumptions: RETURN, XpmCalloc, XpmMalloc, XpmFree, CountExtensions, CreateColors, CreatePixels, CreateExtensions are external macros/functions; RETURN is taken to set ErrorStatus and jump to the exit label, per the `exit:` block at the end of the function.
XpmCreateDataFromXpmImage is a non-static exported library API, so its `image`/`info` parameters are attacker-data per the data-origin impact model; no caller-side validation is assumed.
limitations: Lines 93 and 95 contain orphaned, syntactically unconditional `RETURN(XpmNoMemory);` statements that are the residue of a removed overflow-guard condition (`if (image->height > UINT_MAX - offset || image->height * offset >= UINT_MAX - data_size)`) and the removed `if (!data)` allocation NULL-check; under a strictly literal control-flow reading they terminate the function (fail-closed) before line 105. They are treated as corruption artifacts of the removed statements rather than as intended control flow, since the code between them (duplicate `data_size += image->height * offset;` and the pointer-array setup) is only meaningful if execution continues.

Secondary candidate not made primary: no check bounds `image->height * offset` before `data_size += image->height * offset;` (lines 94/96), so `image->height * image->cpp + 1` can wrap `unsigned int` and undersize the computed buffer. Its claimed impact (undersized heap allocation → overflow in CreatePixels/strcpy) is not instantiated in this code because the allocation statement itself is missing; if the allocation were restored without restoring the check, this would be a CWE-190/CWE-787 heap overflow.
The duplicated `data_size += image->height * offset;` (lines 94 and 96) double-counts pixel storage; consequence is over-allocation only, no security impact.

The copy loop condition `l <= n` performs n+1 iterations copying header[0..ncolors], which exactly matches header_nlines = 1 + ncolors — off-by-one was checked and is not a defect here, but note `*(sptr + 1)` at the last iteration writes data[n+1], one slot past the pixel/ext pointer region when height and ext_nlines are both 0.

All other candidates require values produced by not-shown code (header loader consistency, xlateTags table contents, caller-provided msg pointer) and could not be instantiated.

assumptions: The xlateTags table (entries, xtag values, count fields, and the {0,...} terminator that bounds the for loop) is defined outside the given code — UNSOURCED.
Callers pass a valid, initialized 'msg' pointer; no attacker-controllable path reaches msg, and no contract is quotable in the given code.

This function processes untrusted rpm package content (deployment context inferred, not quoted).
limitations: An out-of-bounds read inside headerPut would require the signature header to store an entry whose count exceeds its actual data region; that inconsistency can only be produced by the not-shown header loader, so the precondition is UNSOURCED and the impact link lies in not-shown code.

The 'break' on 'headerIsEntry(h, xl->xtag)' aborts the merge and reports 'invalid signature tag' when the main header already contains a translated tag; within this code the only consequence is a fail-closed error return (xl->stag nonzero). Any caller-side mishandling of that return is not shown, so no fail-open impact could be instantiated.
The error message names xl->xtag rather than the failing xl->stag — cosmetic misattribution only, not security-state misrepresentation (an error is still reported on every failure path).

Allowing counts up to 16 Mi elements permits copies up to ~128 MiB, but the data must already exist in the input package (MINMEM points into sigh's blob), so there is no amplification beyond input size.
Candidates depending on specific xlateTags contents (e.g., duplicate xtag entries or a non-terminated table) cannot be evaluated because the table is UNSOURCED.

verdict.summary: No instantiated vulnerability. argv[1] content is attacker data, but every sink it reaches is guarded by this code's own statements: strcpy's destination is allocated from the identical expression strlen(argv[1]) + 1, so the copy fits exactly (including the empty-string edge); trim_spaces indexes str[len-1] only under the loop condition 'while (len > 0 && ...)', which covers the first and every later access (len==0 and all-space strings exit safely); each buffer is freed exactly once with no use after free; no uninitialized value reaches output or control flow. The remaining gaps — unchecked malloc results (NULL deref at strcpy(buf2, argv[1]) on allocation failure) and the size_t-to-int truncation in 'int len = strlen(str)' — have triggers that cannot be instantiated from this code's input surface (an argv string is OS-capped far below both the allocation-failure scale and INT_MAX, and a negative len makes the loop skip access, failing safe), so they are recorded as limitations, not findings.

assumptions: The process argument vector is bounded by the operating system's per-argument length cap (e.g., MAX_ARG_STRLEN ~128 KiB on Linux), so strlen(argv[1]) is far below INT_MAX and small enough that malloc normally succeeds; this bounds the truncation and allocation-failure candidates.

The doc comment '/** Given a user-input string, remove the trailing spaces from the string. The string should be modified in place. */' documents the precondition that trim_spaces receives a NUL-terminated string; NULL or non-terminated arguments from unseen callers are outside this code's flow.
limitations: Unchecked allocation results: 'char* buf2 = malloc(strlen(argv[1]) + 1);' is followed by 'strcpy(buf2, argv[1]);' and later 'trim_spaces(buf2);' with no NULL test. If malloc returned NULL this would crash (CWE-476-style), but triggering requires allocation failure at a size (~128 KB max per argv string) the attacker cannot force through this code's input surface — environment/OS failure, so not promoted to a finding.

'int len = strlen(str);' truncates size_t to int. A string longer than INT_MAX would yield a negative len; the loop 'while (len > 0 && ...)' then skips all access (fail-safe), and no string of that length is reachable from argv within this code.
trim_spaces performs no NULL check on 'str'; within this code the only caller passes a valid heap copy, and the documented string contract is quoted in the doc comment.

verdict.summary: smacker_read_header allocates attacker-sized frame tables (av_malloc of smk->frames*4, up to ~64MB, and smk->frames, up to ~16MB, from a single 4-byte file field) without checking the allocation results, then dereferences them in the frame-table read loops (smk->frm_size[i] = get_le32(pb); / smk->frm_flags[i] = get_byte(pb);), causing a NULL-pointer write and process crash (denial of service) when the attacker-forced allocation fails.

evidence.reason: Root cause: unchecked av_malloc results for attacker-controlled sizes (frames up to 0xFFFFFF passes the line-32 guard exactly at its limit, demanding 64MB+16MB) are dereferenced at line 41 (and line 44) with no NULL test on any path — unlike the code's own checks 'if (!st) return -1;' and 'if(!st->codec->extradata)'. Instantiated trigger: file with frames=0xFFFFFF → av_malloc(0x3FFFFFC) returns NULL under memory pressure → smk->frm_size[0] = get_le32(pb) writes file data through NULL → SIGSEGV, crashing the process that parses the untrusted file.

evidence.snippet: smk->frames = get_le32(pb);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: smk->frames is read directly from the untrusted input file and flows unchecked into the av_malloc size arguments at lines 36-37 and the dereference loops at lines 40-44.

assumptions: The SmackerContext struct definition is not given; declared types of smk->frames, smk->treesize, smk->frm_size, smk->frm_flags are unsourced — analysis relied only on expression-level types visible in this code.
Standard FFmpeg semantics assumed: get_le32/get_byte read from the ByteIOContext (EOF-safe), av_malloc returns a pointer or NULL, av_new_stream returns a stream pointer or NULL.
smacker_read_header is a demuxer header callback consuming file content, i.e., an untrusted-origin intake point; deployment context is not used as evidence.
limitations: Signed integer overflow: line 61 'smk->pts_inc *= 100;' overflows int for attacker values > 21474836 (e.g. 0x20000000 wraps to INT_MIN), and line 60 'smk->pts_inc = -smk->pts_inc;' is UB for INT_MIN; the trigger is fully attacker-instantiated, but the only characterizable consequence is a corrupted timebase via the not-shown av_reduce/av_set_pts_info (lines 63-64) — degraded timestamps with no characterizable memory-safety, bypass, or misrepresentation impact, so it is recorded here rather than as a finding.

Unchecked av_new_stream result: line 69 'ast[i] = av_new_stream(s, 0);' is dereferenced at line 70 without a NULL check (contrast 'if (!st)' line 48), but triggering it requires failure of a fixed-size allocation the attacker cannot influence in magnitude — environment-dependent failure.

Negative smk->frames (if the struct field is signed) would bypass the '> 0xFFFFFF' check but causes zero loop iterations in this code; the struct field type is UNSOURCED and no use is reached within this function.

If av_malloc fails partially into the header parse, frm_size/frm_flags NULL remain stored in the demuxer context; any later use in smacker_read_packet (not shown) is uncharacterizable, though the crash is already realized at line 41.

verdict.summary: rv10_decode_packet validates the attacker-controlled slice header values (mb_count, s->mb_x, s->mb_y) only by logging errors ('HEADER ERROR', 'POS ERROR', 'COUNT ERROR') without returning or clamping, then runs the decode loop `for(s->mb_num_left= mb_count; ...)` with no bound tying mb_y to s->mb_height. A crafted RV10/RV20 packet whose header declares more macroblocks than remain in the frame drives s->mb_x/s->mb_y past the frame dimensions, and MPV_decode_mb (and ff_h263_decode_mb/ff_update_block_index) then write decoded macroblock data past the allocated picture buffer — an attacker-controlled heap out-of-bounds write.

evidence.reason: The code detects both out-of-frame start positions and mb_count exceeding the remaining macroblocks (left), but every error arm contains only av_log — no return, break, clamp, or rejection on any path. The invariant the decode loop requires (mb_count <= left and mb_x/mb_y within the frame) is therefore never enforced, letting attacker header values proceed to the decode loop.

evidence.snippet: for(s->mb_num_left= mb_count; s->mb_num_left>0; s->mb_num_left--) {
evidence.reason: Loop bound is the unvalidated, attacker-controlled mb_count from the picture-header parse (lines 8/10). With mb_count > left (e.g., 100000 vs left=256), the loop runs far past the end of the frame.

Sink: MPV_decode_mb writes the decoded macroblock into the current picture at (s->mb_x, s->mb_y). The only position update wraps mb_x but increments s->mb_y with no comparison against s->mb_height anywhere in the loop, so after the frame's last macroblock row the next iteration writes attacker-decoded data past the allocated frame buffer (out-of-bounds write); the same holds for the POS ERROR path where mb_x >= mb_width means the wrap never fires.

assumptions: MPV_decode_mb, ff_h263_decode_mb, ff_update_block_index and ff_init_block_index are characterized per the CALLEE BOUNDARY RULE as operating on the macroblock at (s->mb_x, s->mb_y) within the current frame allocated for mb_width x mb_height macroblocks; exceeding those coordinates writes outside the frame allocation.

rv10_decode_picture_header / rv20_decode_picture_header assign s->mb_x, s->mb_y and return mb_count from the attacker-controlled bitstream (they are the parsers of buf, initialized at line 6); their exact code is not shown.
limitations: Fail-open on frame start: line 29-30 'if(MPV_frame_start(s, avctx) < 0)' is followed by ff_er_frame_start(s) instead of an error return, so decoding continues against an unstarted frame; the trigger requires MPV_frame_start to fail (allocation failure), which no attacker input is shown to induce, so it is recorded here rather than as a primary finding.

Line 6 'buf_size*8' can overflow signed int for buf_size >= 2^28 (or a negative buf_size), feeding a corrupted size to init_get_bits (not shown); reachability depends on the caller supplying such a size, so it is not counted as a primary finding.

s->mb_width and s->mb_height have no assignment in this code (set at decoder init) and are UNSOURCED; the confirmed defect does not depend on their concrete values, since mb_count > left is attacker-chosen and unenforced for any frame size.

Line 92 ff_er_add_slice receives possibly out-of-range slice coordinates (s->mb_x-1, s->mb_y); this is a secondary manifestation of the same unvalidated-header root cause and is covered by the primary finding.

verdict.summary: No instantiated vulnerability in the given code. All uses of attacker-controlled SMTP line content are guarded by quoted checks verified in execution order: `if (line == NULL)` before the `*line` dereference; `if (*line != '<')` rejects empty/malformed input; `if (e == NULL) return (0)` before the first use of `e`; the in-place NUL write and the space-skip loop cannot pass the still-present string terminator; `if (!text_to_mailaddr(...)) return (0)` tests the failure sentinel before any field read; `if (p != NULL)` guards the memmove, whose length `strlen(p)+1` is provably within the same buffer since `p` points inside `maddr->user`; the empty return-path acceptance is restricted to MAIL FROM with both parts empty and is followed by unconditional rejection of empty user parts on the RCPT path; and the domain default copy is bounded by `sizeof(maddr->domain)` and re-validated by `valid_domainpart`. Residual risks — NULL `args`/`maddr` (unguarded but unsourced), possible defects in the not-shown `text_to_mailaddr`, NUL-termination of the caller's `line`, and the first-'>' truncation of quoted local parts — could not be instantiated from this code's input surface.

assumptions: `text_to_mailaddr`, `valid_localpart`, and `valid_domainpart` are not shown; this analysis assumes standard semantics (parse-and-copy with NUL-terminated results, boolean validators) and characterizes no defect inside them.
`line` is assumed NUL-terminated (required by `strchr`); no statement in this code enforces it.
`maddr` is assumed to point to a valid `struct mailaddr` whose `user`/`domain` members are fixed-size arrays (implied by `sizeof(maddr->domain)`).
`domain` is a configuration constant not derived from attacker input.
limitations: C1: `*args = e;` (line 21) dereferences `args` with no NULL check anywhere in the code (CWE-476 shape); trigger requires a caller passing NULL, which is UNSOURCED — the attacker controls only the string content, not the pointer arguments — so it is speculative, not a finding.
C2: `maddr == NULL` would fault inside the not-shown `text_to_mailaddr` or at `maddr->user[0]`; the NULL value is UNSOURCED from this code's input surface.

C3: `strchr(maddr->user, ':')`, `strlen(p) + 1`, and the `[0]` reads assume `text_to_mailaddr` NUL-terminates and bounds-fills `maddr->user`/`maddr->domain`; a defect there lives in code not given and cannot be characterized.
C4: an out-of-bounds read in `strchr(line, '>')` requires a non-terminated `line`; the termination contract is a caller precondition this code neither documents nor checks — UNSOURCED.

C5: `e = strchr(line, '>')` truncates at the first '>', which an attacker can place inside a quoted local part (e.g. `<"a>b"@x>`), so the parsed address may differ from the sender's intent (`text_to_mailaddr` receives `"a`, `*args` receives `b"@x>`); the downstream consequence depends on the not-shown callee and delivery code and is not instantiated here.

C6: `strlcpy(maddr->domain, domain, sizeof(maddr->domain))` silently truncates an over-long configured `domain`, after which the truncated value is validated and accepted; `domain` is config this code never assigns (UNSOURCED) and not attacker-controlled.

verdict.summary: smacker_read_header parses an untrusted media file without rejecting an oversized frame count: the check `if(smk->frames > 0xFFFFFF)` only logs (no return in the given code), so `smk->frm_size = av_malloc(smk->frames * 4)` sizes the buffer from a 32-bit-wrapped product (e.g. frames=0x40000000 gives size 0), and the loop `for(i = 0; i < smk->frames; i++) smk->frm_size[i] = get_le32(pb);` then writes up to frames*4 bytes into that undersized (or NULL, unchecked) allocation — a heap out-of-bounds write with attacker-controlled extent and data, i.e. memory corruption from a crafted file.

evidence.snippet:
for(i = 0; i < smk->frames; i++) {
        smk->frm_size[i] = get_le32(pb);
evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink: the loop bound is the raw attacker-controlled frame count with no cap, while the destination was allocated at line 29 from the wrapped product smk->frames*4. With frames=0x40000000 the product wraps to 0, so the very first iteration writes attacker-derived 32-bit values past a zero/minimal (or NULL, unchecked) heap allocation; the write continues for up to 2^30 iterations.

evidence.snippet: smk->frm_size = av_malloc(smk->treesize = get_le32(pb) /* placeholder */);
evidence.reason: Defective computation: `av_malloc(smk->frames * 4)` overflows in 32-bit arithmetic for frames >= 0x20000000 (frames=0x40000000 -> size 0; frames=0x60000000 -> size 2 GiB against a 6 GiB write extent). The allocation size and the loop's write extent diverge after the wrap, and the returned pointer is never NULL-checked before first use at line 34.

evidence.snippet:
if(smk->frames > 0xFFFFFF) {
        av_log(s, AV_LOG_ERROR, "Too many frames: %i\n", smk->frames);
evidence.reason: The only bound on smk->frames contains just an av_log in the given code — no return, clamp, or rejection follows it — so frame counts up to INT_MAX (and negative values, which the `>` comparison also misses) flow on to the allocation and the write loops. This is the missing-check site that instantiates the trigger.

evidence.snippet: smk->frames = get_le32(pb);
evidence.reason: Taint origin: the 32-bit frame count is read directly from the untrusted media file at the demuxer's intake point; any value in [0, 0xFFFFFFFF] is attacker-chosen and no upstream validation is quotable in this code.

assumptions: The given text is syntactically incomplete: the closing braces of several if-blocks and of the function body are absent (evidently removed together with the return statements those blocks contained). Control flow is analyzed as sequential fall-through after each logging check — the only reading consistent with the given text; in particular the blocks at lines 27-28 and 73-76 are treated as non-returning.

Struct member types (SmackerContext) are not shown; smk->frames is treated as a 32-bit integer consistent with its get_le32 producer and the `int i < smk->frames` comparison. smk->treesize likewise holds the full 32-bit file value.

Per the CALLEE BOUNDARY RULE: av_malloc/av_new_stream return a pointer or NULL; get_le32 reads a 32-bit little-endian value from the file; get_buffer(pb, buf, size) copies up to size bytes into buf and returns the copied count (0 for size <= 0).
limitations: extradata NULL fail-open (lines 71-77): if av_malloc(smk->treesize + 16) fails, the error block at lines 73-76 logs and frees but has no return, so line 77 calls get_buffer through a NULL extradata (CWE-476 pattern). The trigger requires a multi-gigabyte allocation to actually fail, which is environment-dependent (deterministic only on 32-bit or ulimited hosts) — speculative, not counted as primary.

treesize+16 wrap cases (treesize in [0xFFFFFFF1, 0xFFFFFFFF] giving extradata < 16 bytes before the int32 writes at lines 82-85) are dismissed: get_buffer returns 0 for the negative size, so the short-read check at line 78 fires `return AVERROR_IO;` (line 81) before those writes execute.
av_new_stream results st (lines 38-40) and ast[i] (lines 59-60) are dereferenced with no NULL check; failure requires OOM not instantiable from file content — speculative.

The magic check at line 10 has no rejecting arm in the given text, so non-SMK files are parsed (validation gap), but no direct memory-safety consequence was instantiated within this code's own statements.
pts_inc = INT_MIN makes `-smk->pts_inc` (line 49) overflow and pass a negative value to av_reduce/av_set_pts_info (lines 53-54), whose behavior is not shown — uncharacterizable link.
Negative smk->frames passes the `> 0xFFFFFF` check and yields NULL/huge allocations, but the loops are skipped and those buffers are unused in this function; later demux code is not shown.

verdict.summary: SetClipboardText interpolates the caller-controlled string `text` directly into a JavaScript string literal passed to emscripten_run_script without any escaping or neutralization. A text value containing a single quote (e.g., "x'); <arbitrary JS>; ('") closes the string literal and injects attacker-chosen JavaScript that executes in the page context, since the function is an exported entry point whose parameter content is untrusted and no guard of any form exists on the PLATFORM_WEB path.

display_dollar() only clamps its column parameter against negative values ('colnr_T col = col_arg < 0 ? 0 : col_arg;') and never bounds it against the current line length before computing 'p + col' and passing it to mb_head_off() for dereference. Any column value greater than the line length (up to INT_MAX, the computed maximum of col) causes mb_head_off to read past the end of the line buffer returned by ml_get_curline(): an attacker-controlled out-of-bounds read (crash/heap disclosure).

evidence.snippet:
p = ml_get_curline();
	curwin->w_cursor.col -= (*mb_head_off)(p, p + col);
evidence.reason: Sink: 'p + col' is passed to mb_head_off, which must dereference at/near that pointer to find the multibyte head (per the code's own comment 'If on the last byte of a multi-byte move to the first byte.'). col is never checked against the line length, so col > strlen(line)+1 reads past the end of the line buffer; col = INT_MAX (instantiated via the exported function's unvalidated parameter) yields a far out-of-bounds dereference.

evidence.snippet: colnr_T col = col_arg < 0 ? 0 : col_arg;
evidence.reason: Origin of the faulty value and the missing-check site: the only guard on the column is a one-sided negative clamp; there is no upper bound, clamp, mask, or comparison of col against the line length anywhere in the function, so col can reach INT_MAX and reach the pointer arithmetic at line 18 unvalidated.

assumptions: colnr_T is assumed to be a signed 32-bit integer (vim's typedef int colnr_T); its negative clamp confirms signedness.

has_mbyte is a global encoding flag read at line 12 but not assigned in this code; it is nonzero under multibyte encodings, gating only whether the vulnerable statement executes — it is explicitly not treated as a guard making the branch dead.
mb_head_off's need to read the byte at/near its second argument is inferred from its documented purpose and the given code's own comment; its implementation is not shown.
redrawing(), cursor_off(), curs_columns(), edit_putchar(), and ml_get_curline() are external vim functions whose internals are not shown.
limitations: Assigning the unbounded col to curwin->w_cursor.col (line 11) and passing it to curs_columns(FALSE) (line 20) could cause additional out-of-range processing, but curs_columns is not shown and not characterizable, so that impact is not confirmed.

Vim's own internal callers reportedly pass the current cursor column, which is always within the line; per the analysis rules this caller behavior is not quotable in the given code and may not demote the finding, since display_dollar is a non-static, exported function whose index parameter is attacker-data at this code's entry point.

verdict.summary: Within the given code, the attacker-influenced value avctx->width (line 10) reaches exactly one sink, the av_fast_malloc allocation size, and every failure path of that allocation is guarded by the quoted check 'if (!s->vert_pred)' (lines 11-13), which lies on the only path and returns AVERROR(ENOMEM) before any use; av_frame_alloc's failure is likewise guarded at lines 7-8. No statement in this code dereferences vert_pred after allocation, so an undersized or huge allocation cannot cause corruption, disclosure, bypass, or unbounded amplification inside these lines. The genuinely dangerous scenarios (negative/oversized/unvalidated width producing a mismatched vert_pred buffer that the not-shown truemotion1 decode loop indexes out of bounds) require either a 32-bit size_t wrap (platform-speculative) or the not-shown decoder's use of the stored buffer, so their impact chains break at code not given and are recorded as limitations, not findings.

assumptions: avctx and avctx->priv_data are non-NULL and priv_data is zero-initialized by the codec framework; no statement in this code allocates or checks them (no quoted contract in the given code).

av_fast_malloc is relied upon per documented framework semantics: it allocates at least min_size bytes or sets *ptr to NULL on failure ('allocation functions return a pointer or NULL'); its internal handling of huge/aligned sizes is not characterizable from the given code.
s->vert_pred_size's declared type and s->vert_pred's initial value are not shown in this snippet; they are taken as unsigned-int-typed and NULL/zero at init, as required by the callee's signature.
sizeof(unsigned int) == 4 and size_t width are platform-dependent; the analysis assumes a typical 64-bit build for the primary evaluation and treats 32-bit behavior separately in limitations.
limitations: Missing width validation (CWE-20 precursor): 'av_fast_malloc(&s->vert_pred, &s->vert_pred_size, s->avctx->width * sizeof(unsigned int));' computes the buffer size from an unvalidated, attacker-influenced int; no range check, clamp, mask, or error arm for width exists anywhere in lines 1-16 (verified in STEP 5). The consequence inside this code is fail-closed (allocation failure -> quoted NULL check -> ENOMEM), but an undersized vert_pred would be indexed by the not-shown truemotion1 decode function, producing an out-of-bounds read/write there. That impact is not instantiated in the given code.

Integer overflow in the size expression (CWE-190/CWE-131 latent): with a 32-bit size_t, width >= 2^30 (e.g. width = 0x40000001 -> min_size = 4) wraps the product at line 10 to a small value, the NULL guard at line 11 passes because the tiny allocation succeeds, and init returns 0 with an undersized buffer. Trigger needs the UNSOURCED 32-bit platform property, and the harm occurs entirely in the not-shown decoder -> speculative.

Negative width (e.g. -1) sign-extends to a ~2^64 size_t at line 10; per documented callee semantics the allocation fails and is caught, but if the not-shown av_fast_malloc implementation wraps huge sizes internally via alignment padding, a tiny buffer could be returned with init succeeding. This depends on uncharacterizable callee internals and on the not-shown decoder's use of the buffer.

Dimension-proportional memory consumption (CWE-400 latent): a crafted container width up to INT_MAX drives a single allocation attempt of up to ~8.6 GB at line 10; failure is fail-closed here, success yields a buffer consistent with width, and any per-frame amplification happens in code not given. Whether the framework bounds avctx->width before init is unquotable either way.

NULL dereference of avctx->priv_data (line 3) would crash, but no producer of NULL priv_data exists in this code and the function is 'static av_cold int truemotion1_decode_init' (line 1), invoked only by the codec core that owns priv_data; speculative contract question, not instantiated.

verdict.summary: rv10_decode_packet extends the GetBitContext bound to 8*buf_size2 bits (line 79) without ever validating buf_size2 against buf_size, the buffer extent registered at init_get_bits(&s->gb, buf, buf_size*8) (line 6). An attacker-crafted slice that exhausts its declared bits mid-macroblock (ret != SLICE_ERROR) with buf_size2 > buf_size passes the extension branch, and the post-MB overread check at line 82 then compares against the inflated bound, so subsequent ff_h263_decode_mb iterations read bits past the end of the buf_size-byte buffer — an out-of-bounds read of attacker-controllable length whose contents are decoded into the output picture.

evidence.reason: Sink: the bitreader bound is overwritten with 8*buf_size2 with no check that buf_size2 <= buf_size anywhere in the function (buf_size2 is compared only against get_bits_count, never against buf_size). Trigger: attacker bits make ff_h263_decode_mb (line 76) consume the slice's declared bits with ret != SLICE_ERROR; with buf_size2 > buf_size the branch is taken, size_in_bits becomes 8*buf_size2, the safety check at line 82 ('s->gb.size_in_bits < get_bits_count(&s->gb)') now passes against the inflated bound, and the next loop iteration reads bits beyond the buf_size-byte buffer registered at line 6 — out-of-bounds read.

evidence.reason: Origin: this statement declares the buffer extent this code enforces for 'buf' — buf_size*8 bits, i.e. buf_size bytes. The extension at line 79 raises the reader bound to buf_size2 bytes with no relation check, so any buf_size2 > buf_size makes subsequent bit reads out of bounds relative to the extent this code itself registered.

assumptions: buf, buf_size and buf_size2 are packet-derived values forwarded by an unshown caller; no documented contract binds buf_size2 to buf_size, so they are treated as attacker-data per the invisible-caller rule.
get_bits/init_get_bits/ff_h263_decode_mb are relied on per standard bitreader semantics: reads are served from the registered buffer and bounded by size_in_bits, which line 79 inflates.

Line 100: ff_er_add_slice receives s->mb_x-1, which is -1 when the loop exits with s->mb_x == 0 (wrap at lines 91-92 or mb_count == 0 with resync at column 0); the -1 is concretely producible but the impact depends entirely on the unshown ff_er_add_slice internals, which cannot be characterized — chain breaks.
Line 21: s->mb_width * s->mb_height can overflow int; both fields are UNSOURCED in this code (set at dimension-init elsewhere), so the trigger precondition is not instantiated here.

The one genuine logic gap — the local-user path (lines 40-43) returns the accepted verdict even when valid_localpart failed — cannot be confirmed because both its decisive preconditions (empty maddr->domain produced by the unshown text_to_mailaddr, and localpart-invalidity per the unshown valid_localpart) and its impact consumer are not quotable or characterizable from this code; it is recorded as a limitation, as are the unchecked args/maddr/domain pointer contracts.

The unshown callee text_to_mailaddr NUL-terminates maddr->user and maddr->domain on its success path; this code's strchr/strlcpy uses depend on that termination, which cannot be quoted here.
Deployment context (daemon/CLI, privilege level, SMTP line-length limits applied upstream) is not quotable from the code and was not used to promote or demote any candidate.

Not confirmed: the preconditions 'maddr->domain[0] == "\0"' and 'valid_localpart(maddr->user) == 0 with non-empty user' are produced only by the unshown text_to_mailaddr/valid_localpart, and the consequence (caller accepting a malformed recipient) occurs in a consumer whose behavior is not shown. If those links behave as inferred, a one-line fix would be to reject (or re-verify the localpart) before the strlcpy at line 41.

strlcpy at lines 41-42 silently truncates a configured 'domain' longer than sizeof(maddr->domain); consequence is graceful truncation of a server-config string with no security effect.

verdict.summary: No instantiated vulnerability. All type-cast sinks are guarded in execution order (descriptor->IsObject() at line 6 before the Object::Cast at line 11; getter->IsFunction() at line 11 before the Function::Cast at line 18; ToLocal() results tested at lines 6, 11, 18 before use, with short-circuit || ensuring empty handles never reach the checks' second operands). No concurrency control over session->dh_handshake_state or session->session_state is visible; if the library invokes this callback concurrently (not shown), a race could exist, but no interleaving window is exhibited in this code.

verdict.summary: unix_getpw dereferences encrypted_pass (if (encrypted_pass[0] == 0)) without any NULL check. The sole NULL test, (encrypted_pass == NULL) at the getspnam block, is compiled only under HAVE_GETSPNAM and, in execution order, only guards the strlen call in the same expression; after encrypted_pass = spwd->sp_pwdp it is never re-tested, and on the plain getpwnam/getprpwnam paths (lines 46/33) no check exists at all, yet the sink at line 129 is compiled unconditionally. verdict.summary: display_dollar() uses the caller-supplied column index 'col' as a raw byte offset into the current line buffer — (*mb_head_off)(p, p + col) — without ever validating 'col' against the line's length. Because the line text comes from the edited file (attacker-controlled content, possibly empty or shorter than col), any col greater than strlen(line) — or negative — makes mb_head_off dereference memory outside the line allocation: a heap out-of-bounds read. No bounds check, clamp, mask, allocation-sizing, or error arm exists anywhere in this function; the only conditionals (!redrawing(), has_mbyte, w_wcol < w_width) do not constrain col.

evidence.snippet:
p = ml_get_curline();
	curwin->w_cursor.col -= (*mb_head_off)(p, p + col);
evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read via unvalidated index: 'col' (attacker-data parameter, no documented precondition or check anywhere in this code) is used as the byte offset 'p + col' into the current line buffer obtained from ml_get_curline() (line content is attacker-controlled file data). mb_head_off dereferences *(p+col); with col = strlen(line)+1 (e.g., col=5 on an empty line, instantiated trigger) the read lands past the line allocation's terminating NUL — heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125, root cause unvalidated index handling, CWE-129). Boundary check: col == strlen(line) is still in-bounds (the NUL); col == strlen(line)+1 is the first out-of-bounds value; no guard on any path.

assumptions: colnr_T is the project's 32-bit signed int typedef; nothing in the given code constrains col's range.

ml_get_curline() returns a pointer to the current line's text, allocated to exactly strlen(line)+1 bytes ending at its NUL terminator (Vim memline semantics); this allocation model is what makes col > strlen(line) an out-of-bounds read.
mb_head_off(base, p) dereferences *p and scans backwards toward base (Vim multibyte API) — its return is bounded by the scan distance, so the subsequent subtraction cannot push w_cursor.col below 0.
has_mbyte != 0 in any multibyte-enabled Vim with a multibyte 'encoding' (e.g., UTF-8, the modern default); redrawing() returns TRUE on normal redraw paths.
limitations: has_mbyte and the return value of redrawing() are globals/state with no assignment in the given code (UNSOURCED); the out-of-bounds-read trigger requires has_mbyte != 0 and redrawing() != 0. Confidence is capped at moderate for this reason.

No call site is shown; 'col' is treated as attacker-data because display_dollar is a non-static (exported) function with no quotable precondition. If every real caller provably passed col <= line length (e.g., no virtualedit/blockwise-past-EOL positions) exposure would narrow, but no such contract is quotable from this code.
A NULL return from ml_get_curline() could not be produced or characterized from the given code, so a NULL-dereference candidate was not confirmed.
curs_columns(FALSE) (line 19) is a project-internal callee whose handling of an out-of-range w_cursor.col is not shown; no in-code sink for the non-multibyte path was instantiated.

The unchecked return of classObjectOfPrivateScript and the lack of NULL checks on className/attributeName can yield at most a process abort whose trigger depends on unshown callee behavior or a caller passing NULL, with no corruption, disclosure, bypass, or amplification; these are recorded as limitations.

The deployment context (renderer process, callers being generated bindings) is not quoted from the code and was not used to demote any candidate.
No caller of this non-static method is shown; className/attributeName were treated as caller-controlled attacker-data per STEP 1, not as contract-guaranteed non-NULL constants.
limitations: C2 (CWE-476, crash-only): the result of classObjectOfPrivateScript(scriptState, className) at line 4 is not checked for an empty handle before 'classObject->GetOwnPropertyDescriptor(...)' at line 6, but whether the unshown callee can return an empty handle (rather than aborting internally on an unknown class) is uncharacterizable, so the empty-handle trigger is speculative.

C1 (CWE-476, crash-only): className and attributeName are used without NULL checks at v8String (line 6) and as fprintf %s arguments (lines 7, 12); a NULL argument from the caller would crash the process, but the worst direct consequence is process termination with no corruption, disclosure, bypass, or amplification, and no statement in this code shows a party across a trust boundary reaching this internal engine method.

RELEASE_NOTREACHED() at lines 8 and 13 aborts the process when the private-script getter lookup fails; this is a deliberate fail-closed invariant check (abort occurs before any use of the missing value), crash-only, and not attacker-instantiable from data processed in this code.

verdict.summary: MACH0_(iterate_chained_fixups) dereferences bin->chained_starts[i] without ever checking that bin->chained_starts itself is non-NULL. The loop bound 'i < bin->nsegs && i < bin->segs_count' bounds the index but not the pointer; the code checks the element ('if (!bin->chained_starts[i])') and later 'if (!bin->chained_starts[i]->page_start) break;' yet no path tests the array pointer. A caller of this non-static entry point (or a parsed Mach-O whose state leaves chained_starts unallocated, e.g. segments present but no chained-fixups data) with nsegs >= 1 and segs_count >= 1 causes a NULL-pointer dereference at the first loop iteration — an attacker-triggerable denial of service while processing untrusted file data.

evidence.snippet:
for (; i < bin->nsegs && i < bin->segs_count; i++) {
		if (!bin->chained_starts[i]) {
evidence.reason: Root cause: missing NULL check on the array pointer bin->chained_starts. The loop guard bounds only the index i, and the element NULL check 'if (!bin->chained_starts[i])' already dereferences the array pointer. Instantiated trigger: bin->chained_starts == NULL with bin->nsegs = 1, bin->segs_count = 1 (both attacker-data: parsed segment counts / non-static parameter state) → i = 0 enters the loop → evaluation of bin->chained_starts[0] dereferences NULL → crash (DoS) in the process consuming the attacker-influenced Mach-O state.

assumptions: bin->chained_starts is allocated/initialized in not-shown parsing code; it is plausibly NULL when the Mach-O contains segments but no LC_DYLD_CHAINED_FIXUPS data — this producer cannot be quoted from the given code and is the residual uncertainty capping confidence.

Array-size relations (chained_starts sized >= nsegs, page_start sized >= page_count, segs sized >= segs_count) are enforced only in not-shown code; the given code quotes the index bounds 'i < bin->nsegs && i < bin->segs_count' and 'if (page_idx >= bin->chained_starts[i]->page_count) break;'.
The bitfield structs cast onto &raw_ptr are assumed to be 8 bytes each (standard dyld chained-pointer layouts); the struct definitions are not shown.
callback/context behavior is not shown and cannot be characterized.
limitations: 'cursor <= limit_end - 8' unsigned underflows when limit_end < 8 (ut64 wrap makes the check vacuously true), letting the callback receive events whose 8-byte read extends past the limit window; the consequence exists only inside the unshown callback, so the impact chain is not instantiated (candidate CWE-191).

'end = start + bin->segs[i].filesize' can wrap ut64 and 'page_end_idx' can underflow when end < start, but every downstream use is bounded by the page_count break and the bounds-checked r_buf_read_at, so no out-of-bounds access results.
Potential mismatch between bin->nsegs and the actual allocated size of bin->chained_starts is unsourced (allocation not shown) and could not be instantiated.

verdict.summary: ff_h264_pred_weight_table never validates the attacker-derived ref_count before using it as the loop bound and array index. For PICT_FRAME pictures it writes weights at indices 16+2*i and 16+2*i+1 (up to 2*ref_count+15) into the fixed-size luma_weight/chroma_weight arrays of H264PredWeightTable, so any active-reference count exceeding (capacity-16)/2 from the untrusted H.264 slice header produces an out-of-bounds write with attacker-stepped offsets and attacker-influenced values.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write: index i is bounded only by the unvalidated attacker-derived ref_count (line 26), and this frame-replication block writes at 16+2*i and 16+2*i+1, reaching up to 2*ref_count+15 in the first dimension of the fixed-size luma_weight array. With the canonical 32-entry capacity, the instantiated trigger ref_count[0]=9, picture_structure==PICT_FRAME makes i=8 write luma_weight[32][0][0] and luma_weight[33][0][0] — one-past-the-end and beyond — on every iteration beyond, stepping attacker-chosen offsets with attacker-influenced values; the chroma writes at lines 73-74 repeat the same overflow. No check, clamp, mask, or corrected loop bound on ref_count exists anywhere in the function.

evidence.snippet: for (i = 0; i < ref_count[list]; i++) {
evidence.reason: Origin of the faulty value: the loop bound and array index i are taken directly from the attacker-controlled ref_count parameter (active reference counts derived from the untrusted PPS/slice header) with no bounds validation of any form in this code; this same unvalidated bound also makes the primary stores pwt->luma_weight[i][list][*] (lines 30-31, 41-42) out-of-bounds when ref_count exceeds the array capacity, storing unchecked get_se_golomb values.

assumptions: The exact first-dimension capacity of pwt->luma_weight / pwt->chroma_weight is not shown in the given code (struct H264PredWeightTable definition not provided); in the canonical FFmpeg definition it is 32. The finding does not depend on the exact value: the capacity is a fixed finite compile-time struct constant and no statement in this code bounds ref_count to any domain, so an attacker-supplied ref_count with 2*ref_count+15 >= capacity always exists (capacity 32 requires only ref_count=9; capacity 48 requires ref_count=17).
get_ue_golomb/get_se_golomb/get_bits1 are relied on per the CALLEE BOUNDARY RULE as bitstream readers returning attacker-controlled values from gb.

ref_count is derived by the (not shown) caller from PPS/slice-header num_ref_idx fields; per STEP 1 the content of a non-static exported parser's parameter is attacker-data, and no documented precondition on it exists in this code.
limitations: Uninitialized/stale chroma_log2_weight_denom when sps->chroma_format_idc == 0: line 12 is skipped, line 17 reads the possibly-uninitialized field, but the unsigned '> 7U' comparison clamps any value (including negative garbage, which converts to a huge unsigned) to [0,7] before the shift at line 22, and chroma_def is consumed only in branches gated by chroma_format_idc (in which case line 12 executed). No security impact.
Attacker-scalable loop amplification (loop bounded only by attacker ref_count) is subsumed by the confirmed out-of-bounds write, which occurs at small i.
Negative ref_count[list] values simply skip the loop ('i < ref_count[list]' is false at i=0); no separate defect.

The (int8_t) range checks at lines 32-34 and 51-53 run after the indexed stores at lines 30-31/49-50, so the out_range_weight error path does not undo the already-performed store; this is part of the confirmed write defect, not a separate finding.

verdict.summary: qemu_register_machine concatenates a machine name and registers a TypeInfo. The only defect-shaped candidates are an unguarded dereference m->name (NULL m or NULL m->name, CWE-476-shaped) and the unchecked g_strconcat/type_register results; none has a trigger instantiated in this code: the function reads no external content, no statement in this code produces a NULL for m or m->name, and any harmful consequence of a NULL .name or a failed registration occurs inside the not-shown callee type_register, whose behavior cannot be characterized. The unconditional 'return 0' ignores type_register's result but no security decision or security-state presentation exists here. No memory-size, index, injection, authz, or crypto sink exists in this code, so the code is not vulnerable as given.

g_strconcat is treated per documented GLib semantics (safe length-computing concatenation; NULL first argument yields a NULL return), which is the only characterization used, and only to show no overflow occurs for any string content.

Deployment context (who calls qemu_register_machine and with what privilege) is not quoted and was not used to demote any candidate; demotions rest solely on the UNSOURCED trigger rule and uncharacterizable impact links.
limitations: NULL-dereference candidate at 'm->name' (line 4): no guard of any form exists in this code (verified: no NULL check, assert, clamp, or error arm before the initializer), but the trigger precondition m == NULL is UNSOURCED — no statement in this code assigns or produces NULL for m, and this code reads no external content that could carry it; the only conceivable producer is the direct caller, whose behavior is not shown. Per the UNSOURCED rule this candidate cannot confirm a vulnerability (CWE-476-shaped, crash-only consequence).

NULL m->name candidate: g_strconcat(NULL, ...) would return NULL, leaving ti.name == NULL at the type_register call (line 9), but the producer of the NULL m->name is likewise UNSOURCED, and the consequence of a NULL type name occurs entirely inside not-shown type_register, which the CALLEE BOUNDARY RULE does not cover.
Unchecked g_strconcat allocation failure (OOM) leading to ti.name == NULL: trigger requires an allocation failure no attacker can induce — not a vulnerability.

Unchecked return value of type_register combined with unconditional 'return 0' (line 10): whether type_register can fail and whether its failure has security effect is not characterizable from the given code; no authn/authz/verification or security-state presentation exists in this snippet, so no CWE-451 finding is instantiated.
The g_strconcat result is never freed (leak), but retention is bounded by the number of registration calls and no attacker-controlled count exists in this code — no scalable impact.

Stack-allocated ti is passed by address to type_register; if the not-shown callee retained the pointer past return there would be a dangling reference, but this depends entirely on unshown callee behavior and cannot be evaluated here.

verdict.summary: This function (Vim's op_format) consumes only editor-internal operator state (oap coordinates, window/buffer globals), not attacker-controlled file or protocol content, and contains no memory, copy, or formatting sink operating on external data. The one arithmetic sink, ++curwin->w_cursor.lnum, is guarded by the quoted bound 'curwin->w_cursor.lnum < curbuf->b_ml.ml_line_count', and the restored cursor is normalized by the quoted 'check_cursor();'. Remaining candidates (negative line number passed to u_save, unvalidated oap->line_count passed to format_lines, w_old_cursor_lnum/w_old_visual_lnum shifted to <=0 after line deletion) all depend on values produced by code not given (oap population, window state) and on consumers not given (undo, format_lines internals, screen redraw), so neither their triggers nor their impact chains could be instantiated in this code.

assumptions: op_format is invoked from Vim's operator machinery (e.g. do_pending_operator) which populates oap->start/oap->end with valid buffer line numbers (start.lnum >= 1, end.lnum <= ml_line_count) and oap->line_count consistently; this enforcement is not shown in the given code.

u_save and format_lines (callees, not shown) validate their line-number/count arguments and return FAIL on invalid input; the FAIL path of u_save is handled here ('if (u_save(...) == FAIL) return;') but range enforcement is assumed external.
saved_cursor is a global whose lnum is used as a sentinel (0) elsewhere; this code resets it ('saved_cursor.lnum = 0;') after use.
Consumers of w_old_cursor_lnum/w_old_visual_lnum (redraw logic in screen.c, not shown) tolerate or re-check values this code may shift by the line-count delta.
limitations: C1: 'u_save((linenr_T)(oap->start.lnum - 1), (linenr_T)(oap->end.lnum + 1))' would pass a negative/out-of-range line number if oap->start.lnum were 0 or oap->end.lnum exceeded the buffer; no producer of such values exists in the given code (UNSOURCED precondition), so the trigger could not be instantiated.
C2: 'format_lines(oap->line_count, keep_cursor)' receives an unvalidated count; oap->line_count is computed in code not shown, so a negative or over-large value could not be sourced here.

C3: 'wp->w_old_cursor_lnum += old_line_count' / 'wp->w_old_visual_lnum += old_line_count' can drive a redraw line number to 0 or negative when formatting deletes lines (old_line_count can be negative per 'old_line_count = curbuf->b_ml.ml_line_count - old_line_count;'), and the only in-code check 'wp->w_old_cursor_lnum != 0' tests the pre-increment value; however the stale value's harmful use occurs in redraw code not given, so the security impact is not instantiated in this code.
C4: 'oap->end.lnum + 1' can overflow only near LONG_MAX line counts, unreachable given the buffer-line invariants maintained in code not shown.

verdict.summary: All attacker-reachable data (RADIUS User-Name) is NULL-checked and only reaches standard lookup calls and %s log slots; every lookup failure sentinel (getpwnam, getspnam, getprpwnam, getusershell, pairmake) is tested before first use, and all error paths fail closed. The candidate defects (unchecked NULL pw_passwd/sp_pwdp/pw_shell dereference, the OSFC2 fg_lock comparison, expiry checks skipped when the passwd hash is >=10 chars, and the pairmove/pairfree lifetime question) each hinge on UNSOURCED preconditions (OS-dependent struct field NULL-ness, root-configured account state, the never-assigned request->timestamp) or on not-shown, non-standard callees, so no trigger could be instantiated within this code.

jpc_pi_nextrpcl computes the precinct index pi->prcno = prcvind * pi->pirlvl->numhprcs + prchind entirely from attacker-controlled JPEG-2000 codestream geometry (tile bounds, sampling factors, precinct exponents, POC progression-change values) and then uses it to index pi->pirlvl->prclyrnos[pi->prcno] with no bounds check: the only guard is a debug assert (assert(pi->prcno < pi->pirlvl->numprcs)), which is compiled out in release builds and does not reject any out-of-range value at runtime. A crafted codestream whose precinct-index arithmetic exceeds (or sign-wraps past) the allocated precinct-layer array causes an out-of-bounds read at *prclyrno followed by an out-of-bounds heap write via ++(*prclyrno) — memory corruption reachable from untrusted input.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds heap read and write: pi->prcno (a uint index computed from attacker-controlled codestream geometry) is used to index pi->pirlvl->prclyrnos with no range check on any path. *prclyrno reads OOB heap memory and ++(*prclyrno) performs an OOB heap write when a crafted file makes prcvind * numhprcs + prchind reach or exceed the number of allocated precincts (e.g., x=0x1000, hsamp=1, r=0, prcwidthexpn=0, numhprcs=numprcs=1 yields prcno=0x1000).

evidence.snippet:
pi->prcno = prcvind * pi->pirlvl->numhprcs + prchind;

						assert(pi->prcno < pi->pirlvl->numprcs);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted index: prchind/prcvind are derived from attacker file content (pi->x/y bounds, hsamp/vsamp, prcwidthexpn/prcheightexpn, numhprcs) with no clamp, mask, or range check in this code; the signed product/sum can also overflow or go negative and wrap through the unsigned member. The only intervening statement is a debug assert, which is removed under NDEBUG and is not an enforcing guard, so nothing bounds prcno before the sink at line 77.

assumptions: The pi->... geometry fields (xstart/xend/ystart/yend, numcomps, numlyrs, maxrlvls, pchg, picomps/pirlvls members incl. hsamp, vsamp, numrlvls, prcwidthexpn, prcheightexpn, numhprcs, numprcs) are populated by the not-shown JPEG-2000 decoder from the untrusted input file and are treated as attacker-data per the data-origin model; no assignment to them exists in this code.
The prclyrnos array is allocated with numprcs entries by the not-shown decoder (suggested by the assert's comparison target); the out-of-bounds is relative to that allocation.
Release builds define NDEBUG, eliminating the assert per standard C semantics.
limitations: Division by zero is possible in the x/y loop increments (pi->x % pi->xstep / pi->y % pi->ystep) if pi->xstep/ystep remain 0 (numcomps==0, or 1 << (prcwidthexpn + numrlvls - rlvlno - 1) overflows for attacker-chosen exponents); whether the not-shown decoder enforces numcomps>=1 and clamps the exponents is unquotable, so this DoS trigger is UNSOURCED and not counted as a finding.

pi->picomp = &pi->picomps[pi->compno] is initialized from unvalidated pchg->compnostart, forming a potentially out-of-bounds pointer, but the loop condition (pi->compno < pchg->compnoend && pi->compno < pi->numcomps) is evaluated before any dereference, so no out-of-bounds memory access occurs on that path.

Signed overflow in xstep/ystep computation (hsamp * (1 << k)) and in prcvind * numhprcs + prchind is undefined behavior; it is captured as a contributing cause of candidate A rather than a separate finding.

u_save, format_lines, beginline, msgmore, and redraw_curbuf_later are Vim-internal callees; only u_save's FAIL return is consumed and checked in this code.

Invalid oap->cursor_start left in curwin->w_cursor on the u_save FAIL early-return path ('if (u_save(...) == FAIL) return;'): if cursor_start carries lnum 0, an out-of-range cursor persists; the producer of cursor_start and any consumer dereferencing the invalid cursor are outside the given code, so impact is not instantiated.

Visual-mode branch: 'wp->w_old_cursor_lnum += old_line_count;' / 'wp->w_old_visual_lnum += old_line_count;' can drive valid nonzero line numbers to 0 or negative when formatting deletes lines (guard 'if (wp->w_old_cursor_lnum != 0)' executes before the adjustment and never revalidates; the else arm adjusts w_old_visual_lnum with no check). The negative value is concretely producible from this code (old_line_count is a quoted delta of ml_line_count before/after format_lines), but the consumer of w_old_* fields is the not-shown redraw engine; whether an out-of-domain value causes a memory access or only a redundant redraw cannot be determined from the given code.

verdict.summary: dbcs_ptr2len reads p[0] and conditionally p[1] on a NUL-terminated byte string. The early return 'if (*p == NUL) return 0;' executes before the p[1] read on every path, so within the string contract p[1] is always readable; the MB_BYTE2LEN index is a single char_u byte, bounded to [0,255] by its type width, so no out-of-range index is producible from this code's data flow. The remaining hazards (NULL p, non-NUL-terminated buffer, caller misuse of the returned length) have no producer in this code and their triggers are un-instantiable from the given statements.

assumptions: char_u is Vim's unsigned char typedef and NUL is 0; neither definition appears in the given code.

MB_BYTE2LEN(b) is Vim's mb_byte2len_tab[b], a 256-entry table indexed by a single byte; the macro body is not in the given code, but the index argument is one byte whose type width bounds it to 0-255, matching a 256-entry table.
Callers pass a pointer to a NUL-terminated buffer, as evidenced by this code's own NUL sentinel checks (lines 5 and 10); the contract itself is not documented in the given code.
limitations: NULL-pointer dereference at line 5 ('if (*p == NUL)'): triggerable only by a caller passing NULL; no statement in this code produces or assigns NULL to p, so the precondition is UNSOURCED and speculative. Impact would be a crash only.

One-byte out-of-bounds read at line 10 ('if (len == 2 && p[1] == NUL)') requires a buffer that is not NUL-terminated (p[0] being the final allocated byte with a non-NUL lead byte); under the same precondition the read at line 5 is already out of bounds, so this is a wholesale string-contract violation by the caller, with no in-code producer of such a buffer.

If MB_BYTE2LEN could return a value other than 0/1/2, or if a caller advances a pointer by the returned length without handling 0, misuse would occur in code not shown; the CALLEE BOUNDARY RULE does not cover consumer behavior, so these are limitations, not findings.

verdict.summary: vp8_decoder_remove_threads dereferences its non-static entry-point parameter pbi without any NULL check (first use: 'if (pbi->b_multithreaded_rd)'), and no documented/asserted non-NULL contract exists in the code. A caller passing NULL reaches an invalid read and process termination (denial of service). verdict.summary: sanity_check_ckpt accumulates five attacker-controlled on-disk 32-bit segment counts into the unsigned 32-bit variable fsmeta with plain '+=' and no per-field bounds. The sum can wrap modulo 2^32, so the only guard, 'if (unlikely(fsmeta >= total)) return 1;', is checked against the wrapped value and accepts images whose individual segment_count_ckpt/sit/nat/ssa fields each exceed the entire device. A crafted f2fs image (e.g. segment_count_ckpt=0xFFFFFFFA, rsvd_segment_count=30, total=100) passes all checks and the function returns 0, presenting the sane/verified state for a grossly corrupt filesystem geometry at the mount-time trust boundary.

evidence.reason: Root cause: unsigned 32-bit integer overflow (wrap) in the fsmeta accumulation of attacker-supplied superblock/checkpoint fields. No per-field bound, overflow-checked add, u64 widening, clamp, or mask exists anywhere on the path (verified in STEP 5). Instantiated trigger: segment_count_ckpt=0xFFFFFFFA + rsvd_segment_count=30 wraps fsmeta to 24 < total=100, so the 'fsmeta >= total' guard does not fire and the function returns 0 (sane) for an image whose metadata segment count alone exceeds the whole device.

assumptions: F2FS_RAW_SUPER(sbi) and F2FS_CKPT(sbi) return valid pointers (macros not shown in this code).
F2FS_MIN_SEGMENTS, NR_CURSEG_NODE_TYPE and NR_CURSEG_DATA_TYPE are compile-time constants whose values are not shown; the trigger was constructed relative to their value so it holds regardless.

The unshown downstream impact is not relied on for the verdict.

Same under-validation class; its further impact is in unshown caller code.

verdict.summary: In sanity_check_ckpt, fsmeta is the sum of five attacker-controlled on-disk u32 fields computed in unsigned int arithmetic (lines 9-13). The sum can wrap modulo 2^32, so the sanity invariant check `if (unlikely(fsmeta >= total)) return 1;` (line 15) and the later `fsmeta < F2FS_MIN_SEGMENTS` check (line 21) both test a truncated value. An attacker-crafted f2fs image whose true metadata segment count (~17 billion with four fields at 0xFFFFFFFF) exceeds total segments can make the wrapped fsmeta land below total, causing the validator to return 0 ('checkpoint is sane') for a grossly inconsistent filesystem layout - a fail-open bypass of the on-disk trust-boundary validation performed at mount time.

evidence.reason: fsmeta is declared unsigned int and accumulates five attacker-controlled on-disk u32 values with unchecked += operations whose true sum can reach 0x4FFFFFFFB, wrapping mod 2^32. The overflowed (wrapped) value is then compared against total at the `fsmeta >= total` guard, so the guard is defeated. Instantiated trigger: segment_count=0x10000000, the four ckpt/sit/nat/rsvd fields = 0xFFFFFFFF, segment_count_ssa = 0x1000000 gives wrapped fsmeta = 0x000FFFFC (1,048,572) < total (268,435,456) while the true metadata count is 17,180,046,076 segments; with ovp_segments=1, reserved_segments=0xFFFFFFFF, and no cp error, the function reaches `return 0` and declares the inconsistent checkpoint valid. No 64-bit temporary, per-addition overflow check, clamp, or mask exists anywhere on any path, so the mount-time sanity validation for untrusted on-disk data fails open.

f2fs_cp_error(sbi) is internal state assumed false on a fresh mount of a crafted image; it is not attacker-derived and its only effect is an additional reject path.
